shortlist.raw_text: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching 1/ρ_u, where ρ_u is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: ρ_u is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

shortlist.raw_text: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, an associate professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place for humans that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. shortlist.raw_text: In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks. However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score. To address these challenges, we propose R^2Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves. To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn. Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it. Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment. Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R^2Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.

shortlist.raw_text: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.

shortlist.raw_text: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

Title: AI delivers 'zero financial payoff' to most companies, Apollo economist says

Article text (excerpt):
AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).
Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.
Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”
“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”
Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains .

Coverage from CFO.com: "Apollo exec says AI has ‘zero financial payoff’ beyond tech sector"
Though the artificial intelligence boom has helped lift the stocks of a few tech giants, it’s done little for other S&P 500 firms, argues Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok.
Is anyone outside the tech sector actually benefiting from the artificial intelligence boom? A new report by a partner from Apollo Global Management raises questions about the nascent technology’s impacts on the wider economy.
In a blog published Oct. 24 , Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo, argued that AI has “delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech.” Only the so-called “Magnificent Seven,” a group of high-profile tech stocks including Nvidia, Amazon and Meta, are seeing rising revenue per worker and profit margins, Slok wrote, noting that both metrics are trending flat for the remainder of the S&P 500 companies.
“With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins,” Slok wrote. “As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited.”
Slok’s report came amid continuing fears of a potential economic “bubble” in the AI space alongside concerns about the circular nature of deals among the Magnificent Seven companies. One economist at a recent CFO gathering in Colorado even suggested that the U.S. economy would essentially be in an economic recession if it were not for the massive sums of money being invested in the AI industry.
The Apollo blog also came just days before frontier AI company Anthropic issued its S-1 document to go public with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Though that filing showed a rapid increase in revenue for the young company, it also revealed massive losses surpassing $80 billion for the first half of 2026.
Slok’s essay was surprising to see from Apollo, a global investment firm that itself has funded several AI-related initiatives. Just one day after Slok’s essay came out, for instance, Elon Musk announced that his company SpaceX has signed a multibillion-dollar chip financing commitment with Apollo.
Going forward, Slok wrote, the lingering question is whether “mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”

text:
Strip the 7 major tech giants out of the S&P 500.

For the remaining 493 companies, AI spending has produced zero financial payoff.

The numbers explain why.

Apollo Global Management's chief economist, Torsten Slok, tracked profit margins and revenue per worker across the S&P 493. Outside of big tech, both metrics remain flat.

Companies are buying tokens, running pilots, and writing checks. They are not making more revenue.

A survey of enterprise buyers shows what is happening on the ground:
• 55% of companies increased their AI spending
• 23% say the financial value actually exceeds the cost
• 89% had to limit or redesign projects due to rising token bills

Instead of driving growth, software spending is turning into a cost center that weighs down profit margins.

Slok puts the core problem simply: AI is a great calculator, but business is mostly judgment. Current models do not understand context, accountability, trust, or unwritten rules.

My read: tech suppliers are making billions selling raw intelligence, but mainstream businesses cannot turn cheap tokens into higher margins without judgment.

Until software masters human context, the return on investment stays with the companies selling the chips and cloud space.

Which department in your company is actually getting a financial return from model usage?

Source: techcrunch.com, with reporting from The Motley Fool on MSN and Yahoo Finance
alt_openings:
Option 1: Bare number first
Line 1: 493 companies in the S&P 500 show zero financial payoff from AI.
Line 2: Across the entire index outside seven tech giants, profit margins remain flat.
When to prefer: Use when writing for finance professionals and executives who react immediately to market index benchmarks and hard capital efficiency stats.

Option 2: Tool as subject
Line 1: Enterprise AI models are failing to increase profit margins outside the tech sector.
Line 2: A major Wall Street firm found that corporate token spending is acting as a net cost center.
When to prefer: Use for operations and engineering leaders who want a direct statement about software performance rather than macro market metrics.

Option 3: Your X
Line 1: Your company's growing AI budget is likely shrinking your profit margins.
Line 2: Outside seven big tech suppliers, corporate buyers report almost no net financial return.
When to prefer: Use when targeting budget holders, founders, and department heads who need a direct call to audit their own internal software expenses.

Pick: Option 1. Leading with the stark count of 493 companies creates immediate curiosity about who is failing, frames the economic scale instantly, and makes it impossible for an executive to scroll past without checking the cause.
headline: Why 493 S&P companies see zero AI payoff
